title: All for the good (Berakhot 60b)
hookLine: Akiva loses his lamp, rooster and donkey on the road, and so escapes raiders
carry: all god does is for good
tomorrow: a fox invites the fish onto dry land. why do they say no?

lines: WHY SAY IT BEFORE HE KNOWS?
cards: Everything happens for a reason. It's on mugs, on posters, in the comments under bad news, and it can land like a slap. Here's a story with a strange detail in it.
Rabbi Akiva is on the road. A town turns him away, no bed for the night. A wind blows out his lamp.
A cat eats his rooster. A lion eats his donkey. And after every single loss, before anything good has happened, he says the same sentence.
Why say it before he knows?

teach.b: First the end of the story, in plain words. That night, troops come and take the town that turned him away. Akiva is out in the dark field, with no lamp to be seen, no rooster to crow, no donkey to bray.
He says: didn't I tell you? All that the Holy One does is for good. Now the puzzle.
If he only said it at the end, it would be a lucky man explaining his luck.

teach.h: HE SAID IT AT EACH LOSS.
teach.b: But the Talmud has him say it at each loss, while it's still just a loss. Look at the line that introduces the story.
A sage teaches that a person should always be used to saying: all that the Merciful One does is for good. Used to saying.
It's a habit, practiced in small moments, not a prediction about how things will turn out. So here's the solution. Akiva isn't claiming to see the reason.
He's choosing how to stand in the dark before the reason shows up, and whether or not it ever does. And notice what he doesn't do.

teach.h: HE STILL SLEEPS IN THE FIELD.
teach.b: He doesn't pretend the field is a bed. He sleeps in it.

teach.h: ALL GOD DOES IS FOR GOOD.
teach.b: The same tractate, in its Mishnah, asks people to bless for the bad as for the good. The blessing doesn't erase the loss.
Something to tell a friend tonight: in this story, the losses that hurt are exactly what keep him hidden. But the habit he practiced came first, back when all he had was a dark road.

how: Many Jews use the phrase 'it's all for the good' (gam zu l'tovah, or Akiva's Aramaic kol d'avid Rachmana l'tav avid) when plans fall apart; the Akiva story from Berakhot 60b is often told alongside it.

games.q: what does “all for the good” mean?
o: Akiva's line after each loss: God's doing is for good
a promise that every loss is quickly paid back
a blessing said only when good news arrives

games.q: Akiva's night on the road — tap the pairs.
p: turned him away for the night

s: Akiva said all for the good only after he saw he was safe
he said it after each loss, while it was still just a loss.
the page frames the sentence as a habit to practice
a person should always be used to saying it.
all for the good means a loss doesn't really hurt
Akiva still sleeps in the field. the same tractate asks people to bless for the bad too.

games.q: your friend's college visit got canceled by a snowstorm, and she's crushed. what would Akiva's habit say first?
o: it's okay to be crushed; the line is about how you stand, not a promise of a reason.
don't be sad: the storm obviously saved you from a worse college.
wait until something good comes of it, and then say all for the good.
games.why: Akiva said it before he knew anything, in a dark field he didn't pretend was a bed. it's a stance in the loss, not a forecast.

practice: Take a pen and write down one small loss from this week: a plan that fell through, something broken, a door that closed. Under it, write Akiva's line, and leave the space between them empty.
You don't have to know yet what goes there.

wordCard.voice: All for the good. Akiva's sentence on the road, said after each loss, before he knew how the night would end.

orig.note: Aramaic: all that the Merciful One does, He does for good.

carryVoice: Pocket line: all God does is for good, said in the dark, before the reason. That's forty-one of fifty.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 60b (a person should always be used to saying 'all that the Merciful One does is for good'; Akiva on the road: no lodging, lamp, rooster, donkey, troops take the town)
Mishnah Berakhot 9:5 (one must bless for the bad as for the good)
